Since this is a read-only replay I can't verify anything, so I'll just write the module importing from "agentic-3js-builder" and its glow kit. I'm designing a dragonbone soul scythe with a stylized, hand-painted LoL aesthetic, drawing inspiration from Soul Reaver and Spirit Blossom-style weapons, chunky and bright.

It stands upright roughly 1.9m tall, resting on the floor on its butt spike, centered at x=0, with the scythe blade curving forward out of the top of the shaft. The shaft is built like a dragon's spine, with vertebra discs, spinous spikes, gold bands, a wrapped leather grip, and a glowing soul-gem pommel at the base, running vertically up to about 1.75m before the blade begins.

Now I'm plotting the crescent blade as an extruded outline in the forward-up plane, defining the upper spine edge and lower cutting edge as a series of coordinate points that curve from the root near the top of the shaft out to a sharp tip and back.

I'm also adding a small backward counterweight spike near the root for balance, and considering smoothing settings so the tip stays sharp while the curves blend, making sure the cut-corner smoothing doesn't cause self-intersections.

I need to figure out how spikes get positioned along the edge using a path function, but b.along expects a bone-following path, and this scythe might be a plain object without joints. Since the builder likely requires at least one root joint, I should probably just define a root joint for the scythe to anchor everything safely.

I'll set up joints explicitly: a root "scythe" joint near the base, a "head" joint at the top, and a "pommel" joint, then use explicit bone assignments on every part so positions stay fixed in model space rather than relying on nearest-joint search.

I should plan a helper function to streamline part creation with sensible bone defaults, and remember that sweep, extrude, lathe, cards, decal, and stick all accept bone options too. Given I can't test this, I want to keep the API usage conservative and aim for roughly 150-250 parts total, picking a themed color palette to guide the design.

I'm separating the glowing elements—gem, rune decals, wisp cards—from the painted bone/gold surfaces, then figuring out how to place rune glyphs along the curved blade face using small tangent-rotated planes or surface decals since the blade geometry isn't flat.

Figuring out orientation for placing rune glyph planes along the path, using frame data (position and tangent axis) so each glyph's "up" direction follows the blade's curve correctly.

For visual elements, I'm planning teal soul-fire wisps trailing from the blade's cutting edge, a glowing dragon-eye sigil medallion at the shaft head, and considering a dragon skull motif for a bone-themed scythe variant.

I'm trying to work out the composition — maybe the skull faces forward at the shaft top with the blade emerging as an extended horn, or perhaps the skull sits at the pommel instead, like a Soul Reaver-style design.

I need to reposition to avoid collision: shrinking the skull and moving it under the blade, with the shaft top lower and the blade arcing up from the skull's back with a clear gap between the skull crown and the blade's lower edge. Overall height comes to around 2.15m, which feels oversized but stylistically fits an exaggerated scythe design.

Now I'm working out the blade's extrusion direction and outline coordinates, defining the upper spine edge points sweeping from root to tip.

Checking the width doesn't taper enough near the tip, so I'm adjusting the lower edge points to pull in closer toward the tip for a sharper point.

I'm checking the convexity near the thin tip region, worried that the sharp converging edges there could cause smoothing cuts to cross each other and create a degenerate sliver.

Now I want to add visual interest to the blade: rather than one flat shape, I'm layering a thicker ivory bone-body with an inner glowing teal "soul-blade" crescent along the cutting edge, built as a second extrude with a slightly offset, thinner outline to create that inner glowing edge effect.

Computing the offset geometry for the soul blade...

Instead I'll just use the sharp tip point directly and skip the inner offset at that vertex, closing the polygon from Lin back to the tip. I'm checking that the inner and outer offset curves don't cross and that the near-tip inner points stay inside the bone's upper edge.

I'll scale the inset/outset offsets by position along the blade, tapering thinner near the tip so the slimmer soul blade protrudes as a glowing sliver from the bone's cutting edge. I also want to add serrated spikes along the bone blade's upper edge, positioned using the catmull path.

Tilting each spike backward along the tangent-outward plane to resemble dragon dorsal fins, then considering radial rib grooves painted on the blade face for extra texture detail.

I'm realizing the shape isn't circular so a constant-radius lower-edge seep won't work cleanly, and I'm looking for a more generic way to fade the teal soul-color near the blade's bottom edge, maybe tying it to the surface normal instead of a radial distance calculation.

Now I'm working out the teal tip tint — blending bone color into teal-tinted bone based on distance from the root toward the tip, with noise added for crack texture, then planning the shaft geometry and claw-foot composition at the base.

For the bottom, I'm shaping a tapering bone spike that touches the floor, topped with a gold ferrule and a small teal gem pommel, then stacking seven vertebra-like discs up the lower shaft using a lathe profile with waisted bone segments.

I'm adding transverse process wings jutting sideways and a spinous process pointing backward to each vertebra, writing a reusable function to place them along the shaft with varying rotation and scale, and planning the leather-wrapped grip with gold bands in the middle. For the layout: butt spike and ferrule near the base, then a vertebra stack with a glowing teal core visible through gaps between each bone segment.

For the grip itself, I'm working out a diagonal spiral stripe pattern using modular angle math to create the leather wrap texture with darker bands and highlights.

Beyond the grip, I'm adding gold trim rings at the top and bottom of the wrap, then planning hanging ribbon tassels with cards featuring purple-and-gold rune stitching and torn edges for decorative volume.

Continuing upward, the vertebrae grow larger toward the neck, capped by a gold collar ring with a teal gem. Then I'm building the dragon skull itself: a scaled cranium sphere, an upper jaw snout tapering from wide to narrow along the z-axis, and a separate lower jaw frustum tilted open beneath it.

I'm setting up the jaw joint hinge, positioning it near the skull and planning to pose it with a positive rotation so the lower jaw drops open naturally, since the lower jaw geometry rides along with that bone.

For detail, I'm planning rings of small ivory spike teeth around the upper and lower jaws with bigger fangs at front, dark eye socket recesses with glowing teal eyes, brow ridge spikes, sweeping curved horns off the cranium, cheek frill fins, nasal holes, and a glowing teal soul-sphere with wisps partially visible inside the mouth.

Instead of soul fire cards drifting from the jaws, I'm deciding to place soul wisps rising from the blade's cutting edge instead, with frames oriented along the lower edge facing outward toward the concave center and leaning toward the tip direction.

I'm working through the card orientation geometry -- facing them along the X axis instead of the tangent direction so they don't appear edge-on when viewed from the side, with roughly 14 small flame cards sized for the blade.

I'm adding small floating soul-orb embellishments near the blade tip, plus ornate gold filigree brackets at the blade root shaped like gripping claws with gems, and a flared gold collar where the blade meets the skull's neck.

Checking the geometry, the blade root overlaps the back of the skull cranium nicely around y 1.78–1.87, so I'm positioning gold clamp plates extruded in the YZ plane to wrap around that junction as decorative bands.

Checking that the plate covers the blade's upper and lower edges across this z-range, it extends slightly beyond the blade boundaries which works fine as a clamp cuff given the thickness difference. This will be gold-painted, and now I need to place the gems.

For gems, I'll add a teal glowing flattened sphere at the plate center on both sides. For the skull's eye, I'm considering glow spheres paired with dark socket spheres, plus a sigil texture on the gold medallion plates - a dragon eye emblem with wings drawn on a dark plane so it glows teal against the dark background.

I'm planning the texture list now, starting with rune glyph sheets for placement on the curved blade surfaces.

I'll generate four single-glyph rune textures with a glowing teal stroke, then add flame wisp variants, a ribbon texture, and the sigil eye emblem, skipping separate gem facet textures since they're not needed, bringing the total to around nine textures with painted leather and bone crack details. Now I'm writing the vertebra helper function that lathes the bone body and extrudes triangular transverse process wings outward from the spine.

For the neural spine, I'm adding a backward-tilted spike extruded in the YZ plane, using a simple spike helper that takes a base point, direction, length, and radius to keep the geometry cheap.

Estimating part counts now: each vertebra (lathed body, wings, spine spike, ring accents) runs about 4-5 parts, times 9 vertebrae gets me to roughly 45 parts.

Now I'm defining the shared BONE paint function — blending warm and cool shading based on surface normal, layering in crack lines from a cellular noise pattern, and adding stain noise for an aged bone look.

Setting up imports from the builder library and glow kit, then starting the metadata and palette constants for the dragonbone scythe design...

Still defining color palette and paint functions...

Adding stains and teal seep tints into cracks for a soul-light effect, then starting a blade paint function with tip tinting and groove ribs defined by angle around the blade axis.

I'll drop the edge-dependent groove idea since it's inconsistent, and move on to defining gold and leather paint functions with shading, highlights, and scratch noise, plus a dark metal core. Then I'm setting up the builder with joints, starting with the scythe root and pommel attachment points.

Continuing the joint hierarchy for head and skull, keeping role tags minimal — just marking the jaw joint's hinge role and skipping the rest since this isn't a creature rig. I'm also simplifying the option typing to avoid overcomplicating the helper signature.

Defining a simple 3-tuple vector type, then starting to build the scythe's skeletal joint hierarchy with root, butt, and head joints.

Adding glow to the core sweep and starting on a butt spike shape, checking that sweep paths and hinge joints behave correctly for the tube geometry.

Actually I like a tripod claw-foot base better: three talons gripping a teal gem orb that splay outward and down to touch the floor, giving the scythe a stable standing pose. I'll arrange three bezier claws in a ring around the shaft at angles roughly 90°, 210°, and 330°, curving from near the shaft down to tips at floor level, with the gem orb nestled above where they meet.

Defining each vertebra's lathe profile...

For the grip I'm setting up a leather-wrapped cylinder between y 0.80 and 1.16, with gold torus rings capping each end using a low-poly ring helper, then starting the upper vertebrae series growing from y 1.20 to 1.54.

Now I'm shaping the gold collar with a flared lathe profile just above the vertebrae, then working out how to hang three decorative ribbons from the lower ring using card frames that face radially outward from the shaft.

I'm placing gold tassel beads at the ribbon ends, around y=0.70, aligning them with the attachment offset so the ribbons drape naturally along the grip without clipping into it.

Now I'm moving on to the skull construction, setting an origin point near the head and building out the cranium as a scaled sphere, then adding brow ridges as small scaled spheres above each eye and starting the upper snout shape.

Still writing skull geometry...

I'll pose the jaw at 14 degrees open, but need to build all jaw pieces first in model space before applying the pose, since posing early would misplace later geometry. Now placing upper teeth along the jaw line.

Working out teeth placement...

Now I'm sketching the eye sockets as small scaled dark spheres with glowing inset orbs, then moving to the horns -- sweeping bezier curves from the skull base, curling back, outward, and down with tapering radius, checking they don't collide with the blade root geometry near the skull top.

Still shaping the frill outline...

I'm deciding to scale up the skull slightly since it's the signature feature despite being small relative to the blade, defining a helper function that places points relative to the skull's origin with a 1.2x scale factor applied uniformly to coordinates and sizes.

Now I'm checking the clearances between skull parts and the blade in these local coordinates—verifying the cranium back, horn tops, and blade root don't overlap after rescaling, adjusting the skull's base origin position to make sure everything fits together properly.

Checking the clamp plate position relative to the cranium — it's thinner than the skull width so it embeds partially, grabbing into the cranium's upper back near where the blade root enters. That overlap looks like the blade mount gripping the skull correctly, so now I'll set the teeth color to a pale cream tone.

Now I'm defining the blade body extrusion with its thickness, bevel, and paint color bound to the blade bone, then adding a thinner teal-glowing soul-edge layer along the blade profile, plus a raised inner "soul vein" sweep running along the blade's mid-curve with tapering radius on each face.

I'm computing the midline points between the blade's upper and lower edge curves at several z-stations by interpolating the outline coordinates, checking each against the nearby profile segments to keep the vein centered inside the blade.

Now I'm modeling the veins in 3D by sweeping a radius along the path with rounded caps and a glow effect, plus placing small rune planes along the vein faces at intervals.

Positioning the runes offset from the vein toward the blade's outer edge, computing the normal direction from the curve center so they sit just above the vein without exceeding the blade's half-width, using around 6 runes between t=0.12 and 0.78, each plane oriented to face outward along the blade's thickness axis.

Now I'm sketching the rune textures themselves as angular teal glyph strokes with a glow, using four variants, then figuring out the spike placements along the blade's upper edge by sampling tangent and normal vectors off the catmull-rom path at several points to orient each spike outward.

Defining the spike outline...

Adding gold clamp plates and teal gem accents...

Working out the plate's y-range at z=-0.09, I find the gem placement at (±0.052, 1.88, -0.085) sits safely above the cranium, and settle on the sigil at (±0.0505, 1.98, 0.05) sized 0.085 as a square with a circular emblem drawn on it.

For the sigil background, I'm planning a dark violet disc with a gold ring and teal eye, using a plane geometry sized to crop into an octagon medallion, mirrored on both sides of the skull. I'm also checking the blade's thickness and clamp dimensions stay consistent with the rune placement, then turning to the soul fire cards along the cutting edge -- plotting them along a curved path from tip to root with inward-facing orientation toward the concave side, sized between 0.07 and 0.16.

Writing frame placement logic...

Now I'm designing the flame SVG itself, layering teal, mid-tone, and bright core paths to build a wispy flame shape rooted at the bottom of the viewbox.

I'm also thinking through small ghost-soul textures—spirit faces with eyes and wavy tails, inspired by Thresh's lantern souls—positioned as cards floating within the concave curve of the blade.

I'm placing three ghosts near the tip at specific coordinates, keeping them away from the skull face's snout, and adding tiny glowing orbs and octahedra sparks scattered across the model. I'm checking the overall bounding box, adding a glowing teal soul gem at the base with a gold curved-bar cage and ring, then moving on to detailing the leather wrap's paint pattern.

Now I'm sketching the ribbon texture as an SVG cloth banner with a violet-to-dark gradient, gold border lines, a teal rune diamond pattern, and a swallowtail notch cut into the bottom edge, while working out how the drawing orientation should map onto the hanging card frame when flipped 180 degrees.

Adding gold border stroke and teal rune diamond shapes at different heights, then checking the stroke scaling works at this viewBox size before moving on to the rune glyph SVGs.

For the inner eye, I'm sketching an almond-shaped dragon eye with a teal fill and dark slit pupil, surrounded by gold spikes radiating outward at eight angles. Now I'm moving on to the tube paints, starting with a leather shader that computes angle bands along the sweep for a woven texture effect.

Writing gold paint shader...

Still writing vertebra lathe geometry...

Still shaping wing geometry...

Still writing blade outline points...

I'm wondering if I should rely on the SDK's exported OutlinePoint type or just declare my own structurally-compatible tuple type to avoid import risk -- I'll define my own local type to be safe.

Now I'm working out the outline geometry for the soul blade shape: computing offset points along each edge by pushing outward and inward from the centerline based on a thickness that varies with position along the blade, forming a closed polygon from tip to root and back.

I'm deciding to keep smoothing at 0 for the soul blade for safety, while using smoothing 1 on the bone blade since it has more edges. For bevel, I'm setting it to 0.006 against a thickness of 0.032, which should fit fine without breaking sharp concave corners. I'm also double-checking the inward direction at the root vertex to confirm it points correctly toward the concave side, then moving to figure out the 3D positions of glow cards along the Lout path using a Catmull curve.

Now I'm placing veins symmetrically on both blade faces, accounting for the bevel so the flat region aligns properly, and setting up the glow shading for the veins as a looping sweep effect. For the flame mounts, I'm generating frames along the soul path with inward-facing directions, then attaching flame cards with randomized size, flow, spin, and sink parameters tied to a bone joint for natural variation and tilt.

I'm second-guessing the flame direction though—hanging flames pointing inward/downward look like dripping fire rather than rising flame, so I'm considering blending the inward direction with an upward world vector so the wisps appear to lick upward off the blade's edge instead of just drooping.

Combining the root-tangent direction with inward pull and a slight downward offset gives wisps that extend toward back-down, and since the axis sits in the YZ plane, the flow vector stays properly perpendicular.

Now I'm adding small ghost-soul cards near the skull facing upward, octahedron sparkle clusters glowing near the blade with varied scales, and gold filigree dragon-wing brackets extruded along the collar sides.

I'm also adding gold cheek guards extruded as beveled plates on either side of the collar, skipping the soul chain idea for now, and double-checking the bounding box so claw tips sit exactly at y=0 and the gem sphere stays comfortably above it.

Now I'm confirming the claw cap geometry touches the floor correctly, considering a gold toenail paint detail and knuckle ring at the claw base, and planning the teal core sweep that peeks through the gaps between vertebrae segments while I work out the y-positions for the lower vertebrae stack.

Still placing vertebrae segments...

Still shaping the skull geometry...

Computing teeth placement...

Now working out eye sockets and glowing eyes: dark recessed sockets paired with smaller glowing cores positioned slightly forward, scaled to fit the narrowing cranium shape near the front of the skull.

I'm positioning brow ridges as flattened spheres above the eyes, and placing tiny dark nostril spheres near the front cap of the snout box.

Now I'm defining the horn shape with a bezier curve, setting control points that curve up and back from the base near the brow to a tapered tip.

I'm checking that the horn placement doesn't clip into the skull plate, confirming the geometry stays clear near the root. I'm skipping jaw spines and keeping the skull painted bone-colored, then adding a glowing teal ellipsoid tucked inside the mouth to simulate an inner soul glow.

Now I'm setting up the jaw hinge rotation—12 degrees around the model's X axis so a positive value tips the forward-facing jaw bone downward, opening the mouth correctly. I'm applying a teal glow effect to the eye parts using a hex color for the emissive tint, and confirming no chain attachment is needed here. I'm also double-checking whether the scale parameter accepts a vector or just a number to avoid type issues.

Writing ribbon frame generation...

Still positioning tassels and beads...

Now for the clamp plate sigil, I'm adding a glowing textured plane using the sigil texture, keeping the dark background unaffected by glow while the gold ring lights up. The rune glyphs get their own planes with white base color so the texture's teal coloring shows through, with six runes each needing two parts for the glow pass, placing them along the vein curve using the catmull-rom path positions.

I'm computing each rune's position by sampling the curve's point and tangent, offsetting outward along the normal, and orienting the plane's "up" direction along the tangent so glyphs read along the blade -- accepting that the mirrored side might flip the text direction, which I'll leave as is for now.

Now I'm setting up the vein as a swept tube along a Catmull-Rom path offset to one side of the blade's centerline, then writing the blade extrusion call with absolute positioning and bevel/smoothing parameters, overriding the joint-based bone placement.

Next I'm writing the paint function for the blade material—computing distance to a center point for ring patterns, blending in a worn metallic tone, using smoothstep toward the tip, and layering in cellular noise to create a mottled teal/dark edge effect...

Writing shared bone shading function...

Still defining the shading function...

For the soul-blade I'm setting a flat teal glow color plus a lighter vein sweep with a stronger glow. I'm skipping the rune halo and sketching out small glowing orbs orbiting the piece, then tallying up the part count across claws, gem, cage ring, core, and vertebrae.

Totaling parts now—body, wings, spine, grip, rings, ribbon cards, beads, collar, guard, skull, blade elements, veins, runes, spikes, gems, sigils, flames, ghosts, sparks—landing around 140, which is close enough to my target. I'm planning to add gold filigree rivets along the clamp plate and gold bands on the horns for extra detail, plus considering rib-like dragon fingers holding the gem.

Adding gold rivet studs around the clamp edges using polygon midpoints pulled slightly toward centroid, plus three thin gold torus rings on the grip and tiny gold vertebra connectors between spine gaps—bringing in roughly 24 more small parts total.

Now I'm setting up the TypeScript module structure: importing the builder utilities and glow kit, defining vector and point types, and planning to wrap texture creation in a makeTextures() function called inside build() to keep paint IDs safe.

Writing flame SVGs...

Still writing ghost shape code...

I'm defining the joint direction for the butt end and setting up the sweep geometry for the core shaft with rounded caps, then sculpting the claw using a bezier path with a tapered radius and pointed cap, painted bone-colored. For the gem cage, I'm positioning a thin gold ring around the gem's equator and placing the tripod claw bases just above it along the shaft.

I'm adjusting the claw curve so it actually cages the gem rather than spreading past it — starting the bezier from the ring at a slightly higher radius, bulging outward around the gem's widest point, then tapering back in to the tip, so the claws visually cradle the stone instead of missing it.

Now I'm double-checking helper function signatures — frustumBox, spike, and torus parameters — to make sure arguments and option objects match, then verifying the gold clamp outline polygon points are ordered correctly for a simple, non-self-intersecting shape.

I'm positioning the spikes along the upper edge, computing their t-values along the Catmull-Rom path so they stay spaced beyond the clamp region and don't overlap the root geometry.

Still writing spike geometry...

Generating spark particles...

I need to position these carefully so they land in the concave gaps between the blade and skull rather than clipping into the geometry, so I'm narrowing the random z/y ranges accordingly.
